card.title: How merging works
card.blurb: Merging is not always the same move. Watch git slide a name forward without saving anything new, then watch it make the one commit that points back at two parents.
hero.eyebrow: Git · Part three · Bringing work back
hero.title: How merging works
intro.0: Bringing a branch back sounds like the big step - the one where git stitches two histories together and something gets broken. Often it does almost nothing: it slides a name forward and stops. Other times it saves one new snapshot that points back at both lines. Which one you get is not a setting you chose; it depends only on where the two names are sitting. Here you watch both happen, so you can tell them apart on sight.
concept.gt-merge.def: Bringing another branch's commits into the one you are on, so two lines become one.
concept.gt-fast-forward.def: When your branch has added nothing since the split, git just slides its name forward and makes no new commit.
concept.gt-merge-commit.def: The commit a merge makes when both sides moved on - the one commit with two parents.
step.0.narr:
`main` and `fix` both grew out of `start the feeding board`. On `fix` somebody moved Mia half an hour earlier, and `main` has saved nothing since the split.

You are standing on `main`, and `git merge fix` brings the other branch in. Before git does anything it settles one question: standing here, can it already reach `fix`? It can - `fix` grew straight out of the commit `main` is sitting on.
step.0.note: `main` is behind on the same line.
step.1.narr:
`git merge fix`, and the name slides forward onto `fix`'s commit. No new dot appeared.

Open `feeding.md` in the panel underneath: the last commit now holds Mia at 06:30, exactly the snapshot `fix` saved. Nothing had to be combined, because the version you wanted was already written down. Git calls that shortcut a fast-forward.
step.1.note: The name moved. No commit was saved.
step.2.narr:
Same start, one difference: this time `main` saved something of its own before merging - Pip now eats at 09:00.

Ask git's question again and the answer flips. From `main` there is no way forward to `fix`, and from `fix` no way forward to `main`. Each side holds a commit the other has never seen.
step.2.note: Both sides moved. Neither can reach the other.
step.3.narr:
The same `git merge fix`, and this time a dot appears with two lines running back out of it, one to each side.

Read `feeding.md` in the panel. Mia at 06:30 came from `fix`, Pip at 09:00 came from `main`, and they are in one file. No commit on either branch held that version, so git had to write it down. **That is what a merge commit is for.**
step.3.note: One new commit, holding a file neither branch had.
step.4.narr:
Nobody has to tell you which one you got. A name that moved forward with no new dot was a fast-forward, and you get one when your branch has added nothing since the split - there is a single line, and you were behind on it. A dot with two parents means both sides had moved, and git wrote the combination down because nothing else held it.

One command, and where the two names were sitting decided the rest.
step.4.note: The shape on the graph tells you which one happened.
